answer: Accounting: the model is a Turing machine whose head moves one cell per step, so one pass over the stored bits costs time proportional to their number. The data has V = Theta(n) stored bits, so one pass costs Theta(n). The transform has Theta(log n) butterfly layers, and each layer scans the whole array, so a standard transform costs Theta(n) times Theta(log n) = Theta(n log n). To beat the log factor, each layer's rearrangement and butterfly work must cost less than one full pass. Two tape procedures do this with a power of their width below one: an interchange of two address chunks of u digits costs O(V u^tau) with tau < 1, and the sifigeg does the butterfly rounds of D axes in O(V d^lambda') with lambda' < 1 instead of D passes. The tape layout makes each transform round a single sifigeg. The widths are small powers of p, and p = 6b with b = ceil(log2 n), so the per-layer savings multiply out to a saving of a power of log n. Why other tweaks do not help: constant factors are free in this model, and the pages I opened do not argue that a different radix or a reordering trick changes the number of layers or the per-layer scan. That step is my inference. The 'only' in the front page is therefore not argued in the pages I read; the accounting and the mechanism are supported.
